clue.text: Play the grande dame? Monsieur is very French with brood (10, two words)

parts.note: M. is the French abbreviation for Monsieur
taken as written
très is French for very
a hen sits on, or broods, her eggs

explanation.surface: A haughty Frenchman broods while someone hams up the role of a grand old lady.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'mistress it' is an old idiom, listed in Chambers, for playing the mistress or acting the lady of the house; the question mark flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting the imperious lady of the household is the sense of the verb phrase, much like 'lord it' for a man.

clue.text: One type of convolvulus or one veg plant 'umankind's dividing

parts.note: Roman numeral one

indicators.note: something dividing another splits it apart by sitting in its middle

parts.note: the pea is a vegetable plant
homo, Latin for man as a species, with its H dropped as the apostrophe shows

explanation.surface: Some cockney gardener explains that bindweed or a vegetable plant splits humanity.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'umankind mimics a dropped H, so HOMO loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ipomoea is the genus of morning glory and sweet potato, within the bindweed family Convolvulaceae.

clue.text: A calypso that rocks? Play this possibly

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a song with a heavy beat, or a sea-nymph on her island
setter's reading: a style you might play, calypso spiked with soul

explanation.walkthrough: Soca, a blend of soul and calypso from Trinidad, is calypso given a driving dance beat; the second half suggests a band might play it.
explanation.definitionFit: This Caribbean dance music fuses calypso with soul, so it is calypso that really rocks.

clue.text: Being on the wagon bottles gentleman up — it was very sad

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means reading from the bottom, so the title runs backwards
to bottle something is to hold it inside, so the title is enclosed

parts.note: TT, teetotal, is abstaining from drink
sir is a gentleman's title

explanation.surface: A teetotaller bottled things up, and it was all very sad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the wagon' is idiom for not drinking. 'it was' marks the answer as obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: Trist is an obsolete word for sorrowful or melancholy, from the French triste.

clue.text: To last, stock must regularly be turned over in stir

definitions.text: To last, stock must regularly be turned over in stir

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the letters gathered so far run backwards
in places those letters inside the word that follows
last points to the final letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written
to roil is to stir up a liquid

explanation.surface: A cook's rule: to keep, a stockpot needs regular attention and stirring.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: stock keeps only if it is regularly boiled again. The middle words supply no letters but complete that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To reboil is to bring a liquid to the boil a second time, as kept stock must be to stay safe.

clue.text: Short time I preserve for part of game …

parts.note: a spell is a brief period
taken as written
to can food is to preserve it

explanation.surface: Someone takes a brief break to bottle fruit before part of a match.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the surface into the next clue; spillikins is a game of picking slips from a heap.
explanation.definitionFit: A spellican is a variant spelling of spillikin, one of the thin sticks used in that pick-up game.

clue.text: … Set tot swallows in gob

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so the second word holds the first

parts.note: a tot is an addition, a sum
to set something down is to put it

explanation.surface: A toddler is told to stop gulping things down with its mouth full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gob' here is a lump of spit, not a mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Sputum is expectorated saliva and mucus, a gob being a slang word for a blob of spit.

clue.text: Stumble on oil dispersed in siliceous deposit

parts.note: to trip is to stumble

indicators.note: something dispersed is scattered, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as letters for rearranging

explanation.surface: A worker slips on oil spilled on a quarry floor.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is a powdery rock of decayed diatoms or chert, a silica-rich earth used as a polish.

clue.text: Broken Esky involving one in arguments at the barbie?

indicators.note: involving means wrapping around, so the shuffled word takes the one inside
a broken thing is in pieces, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: Esky is an Australian brand of cool box, taken as letters
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A broken cool box sparks a row at an Australian barbecue.
explanation.walkthrough: An Esky is the Australian portable cooler; the barbie (barbecue) points to Australian slang, in which a yike is a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Yikes is the plural of the Australian slang noun yike, a fight or argument.

clue.text: Settler admitting 'I'm English' — device for gauging an area

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the settler holds the quoted words inside

parts.note: a planter is a colonist settled on a plantation
I'M as written, then E for English

explanation.surface: A colonist owns up to being English while surveying land with an instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A planimeter is an instrument that measures the area of a plane figure by tracing its outline.

clue.text: Small section opening in part of glomerule?

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small
a pore is a tiny opening, here in a section of tissue

explanation.surface: A biologist describes a small slice through a cluster of cells.
explanation.walkthrough: A glomerule is a small rounded cluster; in fungi it can be a ball of spores, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A spore is the reproductive cell that such a cluster or glomerule is made up of, so it is one component part.

clue.text: Ariel confused about pages, major risk in Shakespeare

indicators.note: about means going round, so the jumbled name wraps around the next item
a confused name has its letters muddled into a new order

parts.note: the spirit in The Tempest, taken as letters
pp is the abbreviation for pages

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's sprite Ariel muddles the pages of a script, putting the play at serious risk.
explanation.walkthrough: Apperil is Shakespeare's own form of peril, used once in Timon of Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an obsolete Shakespearean variant meaning danger or jeopardy, a serious hazard.

clue.text: Medic dispersed bile — it was easily managed

parts.note: a doc is a doctor

indicators.note: dispersed things are scattered about, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as letters for rearranging

explanation.surface: A doctor broke up some bile, and the patient was easy to handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it was' tells you the word is obsolete: it once meant teachable or tractable.
explanation.definitionFit: Docible, from Latin docere 'to teach', meant teachable and so tractable, readily controlled.

clue.text: Expand (as more than one did), and blush follows swimming dips

indicators.note: swimming letters are swirling about, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as letters for rearranging
to redden is to blush

explanation.surface: Swimmers' plunges are followed by flushed faces as they spread out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'follows' puts the blush after the rearranged dips. Spenser wrote dispred for dispread, and this is his plural past-tense form.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispread means to spread out, and this Spenserian form is the past tense used with a plural subject.

clue.text: Wild mango a child brought back

indicators.note: something brought back returns the way it came, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: taken as written
a kid is a child

explanation.surface: A child brings home a wild mango picked from a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Dika is the West African wild mango tree, Irvingia, whose seeds yield dika bread and butter.

clue.text: Prolonged roadworthiness of dated RR — ee, fantastic!

indicators.note: something fantastic is fanciful and unreal, so the letters are freely reworked

parts.note: nine letters taken as fodder

explanation.surface: A Northern enthusiast marvels at an old Rolls-Royce still on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ee' is a Northern English exclamation, and RR is Rolls-Royce, but both are just letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Retreading tyres gives them new tread, extending how long the vehicle stays fit for the road.

clue.text: Cheers writer rarely appearing in a band

parts.note: ta is an informal British thank you
a pen is a writing tool

explanation.surface: A songwriter seldom shows up with the group but toasts them anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' suggests musicians, but here it is a strip of tape; 'rarely' warns that the adjective is a rare one.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapen is a rare adjective meaning made of tape, that is, consisting of a narrow strip.

clue.text: Sally — attractive woman, originally from Oz that is

parts.note: Australian slang for a good-looking woman
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

explanation.surface: Sally is introduced as a pretty woman who hails from Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sally' looks like a woman's name, but here it is the military word for a sudden attack; 'originally from Oz' marks SORT as Australian slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden rush out by besieged troops, which is exactly what a sortie is.

clue.text: Screen vampire, one person imbibing gallons, looking back

indicators.note: looking back faces the other way, so the whole string is read from its end

parts.note: Roman numeral one

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so the second item takes the gallons inside itself

parts.note: as in 'not a soul about'
g is the abbreviation for gallons

explanation.surface: A movie vampire knocks back gallons of something while glancing over its shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: Bela Lugosi played Dracula in the 1931 film, the screen vampire for a generation.
explanation.definitionFit: Lugosi is the surname of the Hungarian-born actor famous as Dracula on film, so he is the screen vampire.

clue.text: Part of compartment is dressed up in metal

indicators.note: dressing something reworks how it is arranged, so the following letters are reordered

parts.note: nine letters taken as fodder

explanation.surface: A section of some container is decked out in metal plating.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Part' as the word itself: in com-part-ment the syllable 'part' comes second from last.
explanation.definitionFit: The penultima is the next-to-last syllable of a word, and 'part' is that syllable in compartment.

clue.text: Fruit stones forming obstruction, found in potty

indicators.note: something found in another is inside it

parts.note: potty and nuts both mean crazy
a let is a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: Fruit pits block a child's potty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potty' is British for mildly crazy here, not a child's toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutlets are the small hard stones of drupes, or little nut-like fruits.

clue.text: Well lining includes line on end of stone like upright slab

indicators.note: includes means takes inside, so the lining holds the line

parts.note: to steen is to line a well with stone
l is the abbreviation for line

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A well's stone lining has a line carved on an upright slab.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the last letter beneath the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Stelene is the adjective from stele, an upright inscribed stone slab, so it means resembling one.

clue.text: Pyrite in the gem trade? Damage box that contains it

parts.note: to mar is to damage

indicators.note: a container holds something, so the box wraps around the final item

parts.note: a case is a box
taken as written

explanation.surface: A jeweller's box gets damaged, along with the fool's-gold stone inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: In the jewellery trade, 'marcasite' is the name used for cut pyrite set in silver, though mineralogists use it for a different iron sulphide.
explanation.definitionFit: Jewellers sell polished iron pyrites under this name, so it is pyrite as the gem trade knows it.

clue.text: One doesn't decline drink primate's brought round

indicators.note: something brought round another surrounds it

parts.note: an ape is a primate; the 's is 'is'
a tot is a small drink

explanation.surface: A monkey that never refuses a drink is wheeled round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decline' wants to mean refuse; it is the grammar sense, to inflect a noun by case.
explanation.definitionFit: An aptote is a noun with no case inflections, one that does not decline grammatically.

clue.text: Continuously having to circumvent US city, regardless

indicators.note: circumventing means going around, so the first word encloses the city

parts.note: as in 'chatting away', on and on
NY is New York

explanation.surface: Someone keeps driving round an American city whatever happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyway means in any case or nevertheless, carrying on whatever the circumstances.

clue.text: Clubs entering old sports car, or copy

indicators.note: entering means going into, so the clubs go inside the car's name

parts.note: the Jaguar E-Type, a classic 1960s sports car
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Golfers' clubs are loaded into a vintage roadster, or perhaps a replica of one.
explanation.definitionFit: An ectype is a reproduction or replica as opposed to the original, its prototype.

clue.text: Grant? Number entered for that will display flattery

indicators.note: something entered goes in, so the number sits inside the name

parts.note: Cary Grant, the Hollywood actor, so his first name
n is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A grant application with a number filled in shows a lot of sweet talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant?' looks like a sum of money; the question mark makes it the actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Carny, or carney, is wheedling, coaxing talk, flattery used to win someone over.

clue.text: Bangle of a kind inscribed in swank lettering

indicators.note: words inscribed in a text sit inside its lettering, so the answer runs within the next two words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A fancy bracelet is engraved with showy, ostentatious lettering.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornamental ring worn round the ankle is a bangle of one particular kind, for the leg rather than the wrist.

clue.text: College book (or books)

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., a college at Cambridge and at London
second meaning: a book of the Old Testament, divided into 1 and 2

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket covers the Bible's two books of Kings, sometimes counted as one.
explanation.definitionFit: King's College names Cambridge and London institutions; Kings is the Old Testament history of Israel's monarchs.

clue.text: Harijan, dead drunk, one imprisoned

indicators.note: something imprisoned is shut inside, so the one goes within the other letters

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for dead
lit is slang for drunk
a means one, as in 'a dog'

explanation.surface: A man of the lowest caste lies drunk to the point of oblivion while another is locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Harijan, 'child of God', was Gandhi's name for the people once called untouchables; the one goes inside D+LIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalit is the name members of the former untouchable castes of India now use for themselves, replacing Gandhi's term.

clue.text: Chamber piece, start to finish a lot of fun

indicators.note: the opening letter is sent to the end, moving round the word

parts.note: a trio is a piece of chamber music for three

explanation.surface: A chamber-music work proves hugely enjoyable from beginning to end.
explanation.definitionFit: A riot, informally, is something or someone hugely entertaining, a great deal of fun.

clue.text: Nancy, or Andy?

parts.note: surface reading: two first names, or the old slang 'nancy' for an effeminate man; setter's reading: the first name of a famous girl detective in American mystery novels, whose surname is wanted; setter's reading: a pet form of a longer man's name, which has a second familiar short form

explanation.walkthrough: Nancy Drew is the teenage sleuth of the American mystery books; Drew, like Andy, is a familiar short form of Andrew.
explanation.definitionFit: One surname-or-nickname fits both names: it follows Nancy in the detective's name and is a pet form of Andrew, as Andy is.

clue.text: Increasingly fluffy, I'll be in a state of depression

indicators.note: saying something will be in a state puts it inside, so the I sits within the next item

parts.note: being on a downer is being depressed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone moping says that as things grow ever softer and fluffier they will sink into gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Down is soft fluffy feathers, so the comparative of 'downy' means more fluffy than before.

clue.text: Like Mme Bovary, having to admit endlessly painful irritation (thing denied)?

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word for admit is cut off
something denied is refused entry, so the bracketed word is taken out of the irritation

parts.note: to enter a name or item is to admit it to a record
the sore gums of a baby cutting teeth
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: Emma Bovary must confess to an endless, nagging itch she is never allowed to satisfy.
explanation.walkthrough: ENTER loses its last letter, and TEETHING loses the letters of THING. The word is French, feminine because Emma is a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers glosses entêtée as infatuated or obstinate, which fits Flaubert's heroine and her headstrong passions for her lovers.

clue.text: Progress limited by some excruciating pain

indicators.note: something limited by another is hemmed in on both sides, so it goes inside

parts.note: any can mean some, as in 'have you any?'
to go is to make progress

explanation.surface: Progress is slowed by a torturing pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition shares a word with the surface: 'excruciating' looks like an adjective on 'pain' but belongs to the definition alongside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Agony is extreme physical or mental suffering, the kind of torment called excruciating.

clue.text: Morse's mini-mouthful having eyed rosters askance? (10, two words)

indicators.note: eyes looking askance are askew, so the letters are set at odds with their order

parts.note: the printed fodder, using only one of its two Rs; the answer has no room for the second

explanation.surface: Inspector Morse picks at a little snack while eyeing duty lists suspiciously.
explanation.walkthrough: A morse is a walrus, famous from the Carroll poem for eating oysters. The printed fodder has one R too many for the ten-letter answer, a slip in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A seed oyster is a young oyster used to stock beds, a tiny morsel by a walrus's standards.
